To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) in vitro, the stimulation of glutamatergical NMDA receptors causes high cytosolic concentrations of calcium, and 2) in the rat nigrostriatal pathway in vivo, the degeneration of neurons is less pronounced in those that contain calcium binding proteins than in those that do not contain it.

the degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson's disease is associated with the stimulation of postsynaptic NMTA receptors and that NMDA receptor blockade protects dopaminergic neurons from degeneration.

1) NMDA receptor stimulation causes a slow neuronal degeneration in vitro and in vivo; 2) this degeneration can be prevented by NMDA antagonists; 3) this slow degeneration is accompanied by cytoskeletal alterations and by the loss of calcium binding proteins; 4) the loss of calcium-binding proteins can be prevented by the NMDA antagonist MK-801.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question whether NMDA receptor stimulation is involved in the slow degenerative process in the nigrostrital system of Parkinson's disease, and whether it is possible to prevent this degeneration by NMDA antagonist treatment.

the question whether NMDA receptor stimulation is involved in the degeneration process of the nigro striatal system in Parkinson disease and whether NMDA antagonist might have a protective effect in Parkinson's disease patients.
the role of NMDARs in the degeneration in PD and the possibility to protect dopaminergic nigral neurons by NMDAR antagonists.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

(a) the stimulation of glutamatergics receptors may play a role, in the slow degenerating neuronal systems in Parkinson's disease and Alzheimer's disease, and (b) NMDA receptor antagonist might protect the neurodegenerative processes in Parkinson's disease.
the role of glutamate receptors in the neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease is unclear and needs further investigation.
the role of glutamate (and NMDA receptors) in the degeneration process of the nigrostratial system in Parkinson's patients remains unclear.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NMDA receptor stimulation plays a role in Parkinson's disease and that NMDA antagonists may protect dopaminergic neurons against neurodegeneration.

the degeneration of dopaminergic nigral neurons in Parkinson's disease is caused by the stimulation of NMDA-receptors by glutamate released from corticostriatal neurons, which in turn is released by the degeneration of dopamine containing neurons.

the NMDA receptor antagonist MK-801 is neuroprotective in the rat model of Parkinson's disease, but not in the mouse model, and that this difference in neuroprotective effects is related to the different sensitivity for NMDA receptor stimulation of the dopamin-ergic neurons in these two models.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the stimulation of NMDA glutamate receptors can cause the death of dopaminergic neurons.
the degeneration of dopaminergic nigral neurons in Parkinson's disease is not caused by NMDA-receptor-mediated excitotoxicity.
NMDA receptor activation is involved in the degeneration in Parkinson's disease and that NMDA antagonists may have therapeutic effects in Parkinson's disease.
